title: After Katrina, a Judge Ruled the Corps Negligent for Flooding New Orleans. The Government Is Immune.
title_candidates: After Katrina, a Judge Ruled the Corps Negligent for Flooding New Orleans. The Government Is Immune.
After Katrina, a Judge Ruled the Corps Negligent in New Orleans. A Higher Court Ruled It Immune.
In Katrina the New Orleans Floodwalls Failed Below Their Design Height. The Government Is Immune.
description:
In New Orleans a concrete wall stands on an earth bank, and the water is nine feet up it. The wall is built for fourteen. At about seven in the morning, it goes.

New Orleans sits lower than the water around it, and stays dry behind a ring of earth banks, concrete walls and pumps.

On the twenty-ninth of August, 2005, the water came up, and what happened next divides into two stories told as one. On the Industrial Canal the surge peaked at fourteen point two feet, above the top of the floodwalls and levees there, and the walls fell backwards into the hole the water had dug behind them.

The drainage canals are a different thing entirely. Here is the sentence the federal investigation wrote about them. Floodwalls at the 17th Street and London Avenue Canals were not overtopped, but failed at water levels below their design height.

At the 17th Street Canal the top of the floodwall was supposed to be fourteen feet, and the water that broke it was around ten to eleven. At the London Avenue Canal the south breach happened when the water level in the canal was eight point two to nine point five feet. The design height there was fourteen point four.

In Orleans East Bank and St. Bernard, about two-thirds of the flooding came through breaches in the floodwalls and levees, not over them. Overtopping was extensive, but would have only occurred for a matter of hours. Breaching allowed water to enter the protected areas for days.

What broke was a gap between the wall and the levee fill on the canal side of the wall, allowing water pressure to act on the wall below the surface of the levee. The water gets into the crack and cuts the earth bank in half, so the canal side is no longer holding up the city side.

There was no room to widen the levees, so the Corps of Engineers put concrete walls on the crests, held up by steel piling. And then it did something better. The New Orleans District made an admirable decision to construct a test section and perform a full-scale test of this type of design, in the Atchafalaya basin, on swampy foundation soils remarkably similar to those at the north end of the 17th Street canal.

This was 1977. Twenty-eight years before Katrina. A gap opened between the sheetpile curtain and the outboard side earthen embankment during loading, and then water penetrated into this gap. This effectively cut the supporting embankment in half. It was a failure mechanism that had not traditionally been considered in the local design of floodwall systems in the New Orleans District.

In the investigators' own words, neither of these lessons were then incorporated in the subsequent design of the floodwalls along the 17th Street, Orleans and London Avenue drainage canals. They ran the test in order to design these walls. The test told them how these walls fail. They designed these walls without it.

These walls were designed to a factor of safety of one point three, traced back to standards developed for levees protecting agricultural land. A city was being held up to a standard written for a field.

Thousands of people sued the United States. The case that reached trial was not about the floodwalls at all. Those were already immune, and the plaintiffs did not contest it. It was about a shipping channel. Bank protection for it was authorised in 1967, and from 1968 until 1980, it is not evident why it was not implemented.

In November of 2009 the judge ruled. The negligence of the Corps, by failing to maintain the channel properly, was not policy, but insouciance, myopia and shortsightedness. For over forty years, he wrote, the Corps was aware that the levee protecting Chalmette and the Lower Ninth Ward was going to be compromised.

On the second of March, 2012, the Fifth Circuit affirmed. Six months later the same three judges reheard it and reversed each judgment for the plaintiffs. Nothing in the record had moved. Whatever the actual reasons for the delay, the failure to armor timely Reach 2 is shielded by the discretionary function exception, a rule that holds whether or not the discretion involved be abused.

One thousand one hundred and eighteen people died in Louisiana, the vast majority in the five parishes around New Orleans, and as of the second of August, 2006, one hundred and thirty-five were still missing. New Orleans has now been flooded by hurricanes six times in a century, in 1915, 1940, 1947, 1965, 1969, and 2005. It should not be allowed to happen again.

---

Prime Documentary makes long-form documentaries about ordinary people and the systems that fail around them. This episode is built from the federal task force's report on the New Orleans hurricane protection system, the independent university team's investigation, the engineering review panel's and Louisiana team's reports, and the trial and appellate opinions.

This film contains AI-assisted visualization: symbolic reconstruction, no real likenesses. Generated imagery is not evidence and is not presented as an authentic record.
